{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-wv-class-e","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"f3fae1e5d059bee802d12f25d6f8624f2dd5058ae6180660514f1f6297064bef","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-wv-class-e:lineage:69","source_registry_sha256":"2261abaab8e2b1aaff5b8a336e3bfcf845adaa75847f0210442061783d7f9afb","source_liveness_sha256":"9a1fb68777f5e9d5c4b27899084cc233b265410fee506dfe6554447a61ea026e"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Emergencies and roadside assistance","heading":"C — Emergencies and roadside assistance","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Emergencies and roadside assistance (part one)

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A01
When checking the brakes the pedal should go no more than halfway to the floor and should feel as if it is hitting something hard, a spongy pedal may mean air bubbles in the brake line, and if the pedal keeps sinking while you push and count to ten the braking system may have a leak [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A01
Check the parking brake by setting it firmly, and if the vehicle still moves easily in drive or first gear the parking brake needs adjustment [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A01
Check under the vehicle frequently for oil, coolant, brake fluid or transmission leaks, check under the hood the battery, engine oil, radiator only when it is cool, power steering, brake master cylinder, belts and hoses, and never smoke or use a flame while doing so [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A01
Tire crashes are preventable, since under-inflated or over-inflated tires and low tread cause safety problems, so check tire pressure monthly with a gauge while the tires are cold against the pressure number on the sticker inside the door jamb, letting air out if the reading is too high and inflating if it is too low [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A01
To check tread depth hold a penny by Lincoln's body and place his head first into the deepest-looking groove, and if you can see all of his head the tires are too worn to drive on and must be replaced [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A01
Check all exterior lights once a month, check the wiper blades at least once a year while keeping the washer fluid container full, and make sure every interior warning light works properly [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A01
A blowout is the sudden collapse of a tire that can throw the vehicle out of control, so hold the steering wheel tightly, steer straight ahead, ease up on the accelerator, do not brake until the vehicle is under control, and then pull all the way off the road into a safe area [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A01
If you cannot get off the road immediately after a blowout, keep driving slowly with the emergency flashers on, and remember that under-inflated tires are one of the most common causes of blowouts [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A02
If your brakes fail, pump the brake pedal quickly, shift to a lower gear while looking for a place to slow down and stop off the roadway, use the horn and lights to warn other drivers, and use the parking brake while holding its release so you can ease off if the rear wheels lock and skid [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A02
In slow traffic you can prevent overheating by shifting into neutral and racing the engine briefly during stops to speed up the fan and water pump, and if the warning light or gauge shows overheating pull off the road, turn off the engine and leave the radiator cap alone until the engine has cooled [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A02
If the vehicle begins to skid stay calm, do not use the brakes unless you are in danger of hitting something, and concentrate on steering out of trouble [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A02
To steer out of a skid take your foot off the gas and turn the wheel in the direction of the skid, turning right if the rear is sliding right and left if it slides left, then if the vehicle starts to skid the other way turn again toward where you want to go and straighten the wheels to regain control [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A02
If the gas pedal sticks, concentrate on steering with your eyes on the road, try to free the pedal with your foot, and if that fails push in the clutch or shift into neutral, use the brakes, stop at the nearest safe place and turn off the ignition [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A02
If your wheels run off the road, grip the wheel tightly, stay on the shoulder, ease off the accelerator, brake gently and slow gradually, then after slowing check behind and ahead for traffic, turn the wheels sharply onto the pavement, and the moment the wheels hit the pavement edge turn them the other way so the vehicle does not shoot across the highway [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A03
If you suddenly lose steering control ease up on the accelerator, and if the vehicle stays in its lane wait until it slows and then brake gently to avoid changing direction, but if it heads off the road or toward a pedestrian or another vehicle brake quickly with maximum pressure [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A03
If your headlights fail on a lighted highway get onto the shoulder or other available space as soon as safely possible, on a dark highway try the parking lights, direction signals or emergency flashers and get off the roadway, and if all lights fail stay on the roadway and slow enough to pull off safely [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A03
If smoke comes from under the hood get off the roadway and turn off the ignition, smother the fire with dirt or sand when no chemical extinguisher is available, never use water because burning gasoline floats on it and spreads, and if the fire gets out of control move at least one hundred feet away because the gas tank may explode [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A03
If a vehicle comes toward you in your lane, move to the right, slow down, then sound your horn and flash your headlights, and do not turn into the lane the other vehicle left because its driver may realize the mistake and swing back [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A03
If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks look both ways for trains, and if a train is coming get out of the vehicle and go to a safe location, while if the oil pressure light comes on get off the road, turn off the engine immediately, check the oil level and add oil if needed [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A03
To jump start a dead battery remove the vent caps from both batteries and cover the open vent wells with a cloth, turn off the lights, heater, air conditioner and radio, connect the positive post of the dead battery to the positive post of the live battery, and connect the negative post of the live battery to the engine block or frame of the vehicle with the dead battery [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A03
Make sure the two vehicles are not touching, start the vehicle giving the jump and let it run a few minutes before starting the other, remove the jumper cables in the opposite order and replace the vent caps, and wash any battery acid off skin, eyes or vehicles immediately with water [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A04
A basic automobile emergency kit holds a battery-powered radio and flashlight with extra batteries, a cell phone charger, jumper cables, signal flares, blankets, critical prescription medications, a basic tool kit, a chemical fire extinguisher, a properly inflated spare tire and jack, quick energy snacks, maps of the area, a compass, a multi-tool and bottled water [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A04
A basic first aid kit holds safety pins, triangular bandages, sterile gauze pads, self-adhesive bandages, scissors, tweezers, hand sanitizer, common pain relievers, antacids, latex gloves, sunscreen, petroleum jelly, mild soap, peroxide and moistened towelettes [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec16-F24 | anchor: A04
About two million people are injured in traffic crashes each year and many of those injuries end in death because proper first aid was not given, so stay calm, do not move the victim unless there is danger of further injury, and try to judge how seriously the victim is hurt [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec16-F25 | anchor: A04
First aid is given in the order control bleeding, restore breathing, treat for shock, then protect broken bones, keeping the victim lying down and comfortable, and you give it when a delay in emergency care could mean death or further injury [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec16-F26 | anchor: A05
Under the Good Samaritan law no one, including a licensed physician or dentist, who in good faith gives emergency care at a crash scene without pay is liable for civil damages from any act or omission in giving that care [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec16-F27 | anchor: A05
If you are involved in a crash stop immediately, turn off the ignition to prevent fire, protect the scene with flares, a flagman or other means, render aid without moving the injured unless absolutely necessary, send for an ambulance or law enforcement, and keep spectators away from the injured [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec16-F28 | anchor: A05
A crash that injures or kills anyone or causes property damage of one thousand dollars or more must be reported to the nearest law enforcement agency, and the people involved should exchange names, addresses, license plate numbers and motor vehicle insurance information [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec16-F29 | anchor: A05
Do not stop at a crash scene unless you are involved or can render assistance, because unnecessary stopping creates additional hazards, and if you strike an unattended vehicle try to find the owner or leave a written notice with your name, address, license plate number, insurance information and the circumstances [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec16-F30 | anchor: A06
The West Virginia Courtesy Patrol, run through the Division of Highways, employs and trains former welfare recipients as operators and dispatchers, assists stranded motorists, removes roadway hazards to reduce secondary crashes, provides gas or directions, changes flat tires, and works alongside the State Police, nine one one centers and other emergency personnel [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F31 | anchor: A06
If you need roadside assistance pull off the highway as far as possible, keep your doors locked and watch who pulls up behind you, and store the Courtesy Patrol number on your cell phone for emergencies [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F32 | anchor: A06
Courtesy Patrol drivers use white pickup trucks with blue and gold reflective logos and a flashing orange bar light, carry identification badges, wear a reflective orange or green vest over a blue and gold trimmed uniform, and approach your vehicle on the passenger side whenever possible [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F33 | anchor: A07
Littering any public or private roadway or property violates West Virginia law, and a conviction brings a fine of fifty to one thousand dollars, up to sixty days in the county jail or at least thirty hours of removing litter, and points may be assessed against the driving record [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F34 | anchor: A07
Dirty motor oil, old tires, antifreeze and batteries are the vehicle wastes that most threaten the environment, because the roughly one gallon of oil from a single oil change can ruin a million gallons of water, stockpiled tires collect water, attract mosquitoes and tempt arsonists, antifreeze is a listed hazardous waste and old batteries hold large amounts of lead and sulfuric acid [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F35 | anchor: A07
All of those vehicle wastes can be recycled, since many auto part retailers and service stations take used oil free, tire retailers dispose of old tires properly, some repair shops recycle antifreeze for a small fee, and battery retailers must by law recycle old batteries on request [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0087]
